```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
options(width = 88)
# The panel, the panel by education band, and the saved outputs of the
# scripts that were run once on the licensed respondent file
panel <- readr::read_csv("../data/europeanisation_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
edu <- readr::read_csv("../data/europeanisation_cy_edu.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(edu3 = factor(edu3, levels = c("low", "mid", "high")),
                          munemp = unemp - mean(unemp), mgrowth = growth - mean(growth),
                          cy = paste(cntry, year, sep = "_"))
analysts <- readr::read_csv("../data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
claim2 <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/claim2_fits.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
real_ml <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/person_multilevel_real.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anchor <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/anchor_person_fixed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
grad <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/prevalence_gradient.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
refits <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/reference_refits.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
years_real <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/person_year_effects.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# the rows of the saved outputs that the prose quotes
real_unemp <- real_ml |> datawizard::data_filter(kind == "fixed", term == "unemp")
real_sd <- real_ml |> datawizard::data_filter(kind == "random")
anchor_cosmo <- anchor |> datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "cosmo")
anchor_b <- stats::setNames(anchor_cosmo$estimate, anchor_cosmo$term)
oa_published <- refits |> datawizard::data_filter(refit_id == "OA_published")
oa_no_interactions <- refits |> datawizard::data_filter(refit_id == "OA_no_interactions")
kevf1 <- analysts |> datawizard::data_filter(analyst_id == "KEVF1")
prl47 <- analysts |> datawizard::data_filter(analyst_id == "PRL47")

# respondents in the panel, and respondents with complete covariates in the

  datawizard::data_filter(kind == "n", design == "published", outcome == "cosmo")
n_complete <- format(n_complete$estimate, big.mark = ",")
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) works at the level of the individual respondent, where the claim of the Europeanisation and the economy case study was first tested. The case study takes its claim from a study by the original author (OA), who reported that poor national economic performance lowers the positive framing of the European Union and fitted that claim to sixteen waves of Eurobarometer respondents with a multilevel model [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]; the [background page](../background.qmd) tells it in full. The respondents are licensed by GESIS and cannot be shipped, so the module shows the saved output of the models that were fitted once on the licensed file, and above each output the code that fits the same model in the workspace, on the file of respondents that you build there from your own downloads. The models themselves are taught in full by the module on [multilevel models](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html) of the Immigration and trust case study, whose respondents of the European Social Survey ship with the course, and this module keeps from that treatment what the Europeanisation case study needs, with a link at each step to the section of the Immigration module that teaches it in full. It meets the module on [panel data](panel-data.qmd), the treatment of the same data at the level of the country-year, at the within–between model of section 4, and it assumes the first three sections of the panel module, on the linear model and clustered standard errors. Section 8 sets out the weights of the case study, the survey weights of the Eurobarometer within each country-year and the weights of the country-years in a regression, the subjects of two decisions of the [specification menu](../menu.qmd).

## 1. The vocabularies {#sec-vocabularies}

The models of this module go by different names in different disciplines – multilevel or hierarchical linear models in sociology and education, multilevel models of time-series cross-section and comparative survey data in political science, panel data with fixed and random effects in econometrics, and mixed models in psychology and biostatistics – and a participant who learnt the models in one discipline can fail to recognise them in the vocabulary of another. [Section 1 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-vocabularies) sets the terms of the four traditions side by side, row by row, with the standard texts of each, so that a reader trained in any of these traditions can find the terms of their own.

Two of the terms change their meaning between the traditions, and both matter for this case study. The first is 'fixed effects'. In econometrics, and in the sociology that follows it [@Allison2009FixedEffectsRegression; @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological], a fixed effect is an intercept for each group estimated as a parameter, the country dummies of the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-fe), while in the multilevel and mixed-model traditions the fixed effects are the coefficients shared by all groups, the fixed part of the model as against its random part, a clash that @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing [p. 245] record: "[f]ixed effects are usually defined as varying coefficients that are not themselves modeled", while "'fixed-effects models' sometimes refer to regressions in which coefficients do not vary by group (so that they are fixed, not random)". The two senses meet in this case study. OA writes of the national indicators that they "are, therefore, included as fixed effects at Level 2 in the models" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 625], in the multilevel sense, since the model has random intercepts for countries and survey waves and no country dummies at all, whereas KQXUE and C6HJR, two of the analysts in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], used fixed effects in the econometric sense, an intercept for each country.

The second term is 'random effects'. In a multilevel model a random effect is a group intercept or slope drawn from a distribution whose variance the model estimates, while in econometrics the term names, above all, an assumption about such effects, that they are uncorrelated with the predictors, as @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross [p. 286] explains and [section 5 of the panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-random-effects) sets out. @HamakerMuthen2020FixedRandomEffects [p. 365] show that the concern of econometricians about fixed against random effects and the concern of the multilevel literature about how to centre a predictor "are actually addressing the same underlying issue", the issue that section 4 takes up. [Section 6 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-fixed-random) sets random intercepts and fixed effects side by side on the respondents of the European Social Survey.

This module follows where it can the advice of @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing [p. 246], which is to "avoid the terms 'fixed' and 'random' entirely, and focus on the description of the model itself (for example, varying intercepts and constant slopes)". It keeps 'fixed effects' for the econometric sense and writes 'the coefficients of the fixed part' for the multilevel one. In R the distinction is written into the syntax. `fixest::feols(y ~ x | cntry)` gives each country an intercept of its own, estimated as a parameter, while `lme4::lmer(y ~ x + (1 | cntry))` draws the country intercepts from a distribution and estimates its variance. Inside `lmer()`, `(1 + x | cntry)` lets the slope of `x` vary by country as well, `(1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year)` nests country-years in countries, and `(1 | cntry) + (1 | year)` crosses countries with years.

## 2. The level of analysis {#sec-why}

A claim about the effect of a context can be read at two levels. In the Europeanisation case study the claim is about countries, and it asks whether the people of a country frame the EU less positively when their national economy performs badly. The same words license a second reading. Perhaps unemployed *people* frame the EU differently, so that a country with more of them shows a lower average without anything having changed for anyone else. The first reading is **contextual**, in that living through high unemployment changes how everyone frames the EU, and the second is **compositional**, in that the mix of people changes while each person frames the EU as before, and a country-year panel cannot separate the two readings, because it contains no people.

Reading an association among aggregates as if it held among individuals is the problem of ecological inference set out by @Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior, and [section 2 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-why) takes the problem up for a claim made about individuals. The multilevel model is the standard way of keeping both levels in one analysis: the respondents enter it as individuals, and the country-years and countries as the contexts in which the respondents answered. Section 6 uses it to ask how much of the national association the composition of the respondents could account for.

## 3. The multilevel model {#sec-multilevel}

Every model of the panel module was fitted at the level of the country-year, whereas OA worked with individual respondents, and so does this section, on `r n_resp` respondents rebuilt from the sixteen GESIS waves. A **multilevel model** fits the respondents directly while representing the nesting explicitly: respondents within country-years, and country-years within countries. With $i$ indexing respondents, $c$ countries and $t$ years, and $x_{ct}$ the unemployment rate of each country-year, the model reads

$$ y_{ict} = \gamma_0 + \beta x_{ct} + v_c + r_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ict} $$

with $v_c \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2)$, $r_{ct} \sim N(0, \sigma_r^2)$ and $\varepsilon_{ict} \sim N(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$. Three variance components now share the noise: $\sigma_v^2$ for durable differences between countries, $\sigma_r^2$ for the departures of country-years from their country, and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ for differences between people inside a cell. The fixed part, $\gamma_0 + \beta x_{ct}$, is shared by everyone, and the random part is a sum of draws at each level. This is the random-effects model of the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-random-effects) generalised, and `(1 | group)` in the notation of `lmer()` declares each random intercept. OA describes the structure with the survey wave as the middle level: "citizens (Level 1; N: 390,373) are sampled within 16 EB waves (Level 2) that repeatedly took place within the 27 EU countries (Level 3)" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. [Section 3 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-levels) writes the model at each of its three levels and draws the structure on a small simulated example.

::: {.callout-note}
## How the outputs of this section were produced

The Eurobarometer files behind the published result are licensed by GESIS and cannot be redistributed, although the sixteen files can be downloaded with a free GESIS account, as the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) explains, so the models of this module that are fitted to the respondents are displayed rather than executed on the page. Every number that comes from the respondents was computed once, on the machine of the facilitator, on the respondent file that the workspace builds from those files with `prep/01_build_respondents.R` (its [codebook](../data/eb_respondents_codebook.md) is published even though the file is not), by a script named in the [sources](#sec-sources) at the end of the page. The code above each output fits the same model in the workspace, once `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` has scored the items into the scales, and on a file that passed every check of the build it reproduces the output, except that the formula names the cosmopolitan scale `s_cosmo`, the name that the workspace gives it, where the scripts of the site call it `cosmo`.
:::

### Levels and evidence {#sec-levels}

The first fit declares only the country level, which is too few levels for these data:

```{r}
#| label: code-two-level
#| eval: false
# in the workspace, after prep/02_scales_and_panel.R, which leaves the scored
# respondents in scored and the World Bank series in macro; the join keeps the
# order of the rows, on which the subsample of section 9 depends
person <- dplyr::left_join(scored, macro, by = c("cntry", "year"))

m_two <- lmerTest::lmer(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry), data = person)
summary(m_two)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-two-level
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "lmer_2lvl.txt")))
```

Read the output in two blocks. The `Random effects` block reports the estimated variance components, $\hat\sigma_v^2 = `r insight::format_value(real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "two_level" & real_sd$term == "cntry: (Intercept)"]^2, digits = 4)`$ for countries and $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = `r insight::format_value(real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "two_level" & real_sd$term == "Residual: NA"]^2, digits = 4)`$ for respondents, and the `Fixed effects` table, which holds the coefficients of the fixed part, reads like an `lm()` coefficient table with one addition, a `df` column computed by the approximation of Satterthwaite in lmerTest [@KuznetsovaEtAl2017LmerTestPackageTests], which estimates how many independent pieces of information support each `t`. That column shows the flaw in this model. A slope of `r insight::format_value(real_unemp$value[real_unemp$model == "two_level"], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` with t = `r insight::format_value(real_unemp$statistic[real_unemp$model == "two_level"], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` on **`r format(round(real_unemp$df[real_unemp$model == "two_level"]), big.mark = ",")` degrees of freedom** looks like overwhelming evidence, but the model has been allowed to treat every respondent as fresh information about unemployment, when every respondent in a country-year shares one unemployment value. The predictor has only 270 distinct values, so a model whose degrees of freedom run to six figures is counting people as if they were countries. @Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel [p. 25] describe the consequence for such two-level designs: variables of the country-year "are implicitly taken as individual-level variables, inflating the degrees of freedom and deflating the SEs", since "[a] cluster-level variable is defined by the fact that it is constant within clusters".

Declaring the country-year level as well changes the result:

```{r}
#| label: code-three-level
#| eval: false
m_three <- lmerTest::lmer(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year), data = person)
summary(m_three)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-three-level
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "lmer_3lvl.txt")))
```

```{r}
#| label: panel-random-intercept
#| include: false
# the random-intercept model of the aggregate panel, for comparison with the
# three-level model of the respondents
m_panel_ri <- lmerTest::lmer(mcosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry), data = panel)
panel_ri <- summary(m_panel_ri)$coefficients["unemp", ]
```

The slope barely moves (`r insight::format_value(real_unemp$value[real_unemp$model == "three_level"], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")`), while its standard error grows `r insight::format_value(real_unemp$se[real_unemp$model == "three_level"] / real_unemp$se[real_unemp$model == "two_level"], digits = 1)`-fold, the `t` falls from `r insight::format_value(real_unemp$statistic[real_unemp$model == "two_level"], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(real_unemp$statistic[real_unemp$model == "three_level"], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`, and the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom collapse to **`r round(real_unemp$df[real_unemp$model == "three_level"])`**. That is the scale of the 270 cells, not of the `r n_resp` respondents, because the predictor varies only between cells. The new variance component ($\hat\sigma_r^2 = `r insight::format_value(real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "three_level" & real_sd$term == "cy: (Intercept)"]^2, digits = 4)`$) is small in absolute terms, yet acknowledging it changes the inference several-fold. The random-intercept model of the aggregate panel, fitted beside it, gives a slope of `r insight::format_value(panel_ri[["Estimate"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` with t = `r insight::format_value(panel_ri[["t value"]], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`. Once the error structure matches the real structure of the data, modelling `r n_resp` people and modelling their 270 cell means give much the same answer about a predictor at the level of the country-year, which is why the course can teach the case study from the shipped panel.

### Random slopes {#sec-slopes}

A **random slope** lets each country have its own unemployment coefficient, drawn from a distribution whose spread is estimated, as [section 8 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-slopes) explains in full,

$$ y_{ict} = \gamma_0 + (\beta + b_c)\, x_{ct} + v_c + r_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ict}, \qquad b_c \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2) $$

and the third fit on the respondents adds one:

```{r}
#| label: code-slopes
#| eval: false
m_slopes <- lmerTest::lmer(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 + unemp | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year), data = person)
summary(m_slopes)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-slopes
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "lmer_slopes.txt")))
```

In the `Random effects` block, the standard deviation of the slope is `r insight::format_value(real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "slopes" & real_sd$term == "cntry: unemp"], digits = 4)`, larger in magnitude than the mean slope of `r insight::format_value(real_unemp$value[real_unemp$model == "slopes"], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` itself, so the countries do not share one unemployment slope. The model estimates that the slope ranges from clearly negative in some countries to positive in others, with the average lying where the earlier fits put it, and the `Corr` of `r insight::format_value(real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "slopes" & real_sd$term == "cntry: (Intercept) ~ unemp"], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` adds that countries with higher intercepts tend to have more negative slopes. The degrees of freedom of the slope in the fixed part are now about **`r round(real_unemp$df[real_unemp$model == "slopes"])`**, because once each country contributes mainly to its own slope, the effective evidence for the *average* slope is the 27 countries, not the 270 cells, and the `df` column in this way tracks where the information comes from.

Two of the five analysts of the robustness study worked at this level, and their results, as the study converted them to partial correlations, mark the two ends of the range recorded for the five. The analyst KEVF1 (in R) reported t = `r insight::format_value(kevf1$statistic, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of about `r round(kevf1$df1)`, converting to a partial correlation of `r insight::format_value(kevf1$r, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`. The analyst PRL47 (in Stata) reported z = `r insight::format_value(prl47$statistic, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` with the count of `r format(prl47$n, big.mark = ",")` respondents standing in for the degrees of freedom, converting to `r insight::format_value(prl47$r, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`. The two used the same data and the same family of models and found the same negative direction, yet their converted effect sizes differ `r round(kevf1$r / prl47$r)`-fold, almost entirely because of the convention for the degrees of freedom. The unit of analysis, and the error structure declared around it, is therefore a choice of **estimand**, a decision about what 'the effect' refers to, and the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-recorded) places each of the five results on the degrees of freedom of its own inference, beside the values recorded in the robustness study, while the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-onescale) shows how much the converted effect sizes depend on the degrees of freedom.

@tbl-levels sets the three fits side by side, as `fit_person_multilevel.R` saved them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-levels
#| tbl-cap: "The unemployment coefficient on the cosmopolitan scale under three random structures, fitted once on the real respondents, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/person_multilevel_real.csv`."
real_unemp |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    `random intercepts for` = unname(c(two_level = "countries",
                                       three_level = "countries and country-years",
                                       slopes = "the same, with a random slope")[model]),
    slope = insight::format_value(value, digits = 5, style_negative = "minus"),
    `standard error` = insight::format_value(se, digits = 5),
    t = insight::format_value(statistic, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"),
    `degrees of freedom` = format(round(df), big.mark = ",")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("random intercepts for", "slope", "standard error", "t",
                                     "degrees of freedom")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

The degrees of freedom of the first row run into the hundreds of thousands, fall to the order of the number of cells once the country-year level is declared, and fall to the order of the number of countries once the slope varies.

### Variance components {#sec-icc}

The variance components of the three-level model show where the variation in framing lies.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vc
#| tbl-cap: "Variance components of the model with random intercepts for countries and country-years, fitted once on the real respondents: standard deviations. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/person_multilevel_real.csv`."
sd_real <- c(cntry = real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "three_level" & real_sd$term == "cntry: (Intercept)"],
             cy = real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "three_level" & real_sd$term == "cy: (Intercept)"],
             person = real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "three_level" & real_sd$term == "Residual: NA"])

tibble::tibble(component = c("between countries", "between country-years", "between people"),
               `standard deviation` = unname(insight::format_value(sd_real, digits = 4))) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2, align = "r")
```

```{r}
#| label: vc-values
#| include: false
var_real <- sd_real^2
```

Variation between people accounts for far more than either of the other components, about `r insight::format_value(100 * var_real[["person"]] / sum(var_real), digits = 0)`% of the total. The share of the variance that lies between the groups is what multilevel modellers call the intraclass correlation, which [section 4 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-variance) sets out, and here it is `r insight::format_value(100 * (var_real[["cntry"]] + var_real[["cy"]]) / sum(var_real), digits = 1)`% for countries and country-years together. The small share reflects the shape of the outcome at this level. A respondent who mentions two things and finds one of them cosmopolitan scores exactly one half, so the score is bounded, takes only a few values, and its scatter within any cell is enormous compared with the differences between cells. That is also why so many respondents add so little precision to the estimate for a predictor at the level of the country-year.

Whenever the predictor is measured at a higher level, a sample size counted in persons suggests a precision that the design does not have. The number of higher-level units sets the limit, and 27 countries are few. The Immigration module sets out what simulation studies of multilevel models find about so few countries in [section 5](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-model) and how the rules of inference count the countries in [section 10](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-few-countries), and the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference) makes the same point for the country-year panel, where CR2 errors with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom count how many of the 27 countries effectively carry the information.

## 4. The within–between model {#sec-rewb}

The [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-within-between) fits the within–between model on the 270 country-years and reads it as an econometrician would, as the device of @Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries that reproduces the fixed-effects slope inside a random-effects model; the code and the numbers of the fit are there. Read from the multilevel side, the same fit is a two-level model in which the country-years are the units at level 1 and the countries the units at level 2 [@Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling, p. 121], the unemployment rate of a country-year is a level-1 predictor, and the within–between model enters it centred on the mean of its country, together with that mean as a predictor at level 2. Centring within clusters yields the slope within the clusters however the clusters differ, whereas the coefficient on the uncentred predictor of a random-intercept model blends the two slopes when they differ [@RaudenbushBryk2002HierarchicalLinearModels, p. 139], as the random-intercept slope of the panel turned out to do. [Section 7 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-within-between) treats the model in full, on a predictor measured for each respondent.

The difference between the two slopes, the between slope minus the within slope, has a reading of its own in the multilevel tradition, as what Raudenbush and Bryk call a contextual effect (p. 141). On the panel that difference is the coefficient on the country mean in the Mundlak form, positive and different from zero under every test that the panel module applies: the expected difference in cosmopolitan framing between two country-years with the same unemployment rate in countries whose average rates over the decade differ by one point, a comparison across countries that a claim about change within them does not ask for.

With respondents in the model the decomposition takes one step more. @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 124] observes that the usual model for comparative surveys repeated over time, with respondents in country-years in countries and a single coefficient on a variable of the country-year, "effectively assumes that the cross-sectional and longitudinal relationships between x and y are the same", and he proposes to split such a variable into the mean of each country and the departure of each country-year from it, both entered beside the characteristics of the respondents, together with a term for time. The published model of OA, to which the next section turns, has the single coefficient of the first form, and section 7 shows what a term for the years does to it.

## 5. The published model {#sec-published-model}

The published model of OA regresses the framing scale of each respondent on sex, age, education, occupation and the type of community, with the national growth and unemployment rates, and with random intercepts for countries and for the `r oa_no_interactions$country_waves` country-waves, the national samples of the sixteen waves, in which the respondents were surveyed. Without the interactions of the paper, which the next paragraph takes up, the model is fitted in the workspace with the reference categories of the paper and the continuous predictors centred on their means:

```{r}
#| label: code-published
#| eval: false
# the reference categories of the paper: manual workers, large towns and the
# lowest band of education
person <- person |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    edu3 = factor(edu3, levels = c("low", "mid", "high")),
    ses = factor(ses, levels = c("manual", "self_employed", "manager", "white_collar",
                                 "house_person", "unemployed", "retired", "student")),
    urban = factor(urban, levels = c("large_town", "rural", "small_town")),
    mage = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    munemp = unemp - mean(unemp),
    mgrowth = growth - mean(growth))

m_cosmo <- lmerTest::lmer(s_cosmo ~ female + mage + edu3 + ses + urban + mgrowth + munemp +
                            (1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:eb),
                          data = person, REML = FALSE)
summary(m_cosmo)
```

The script `fit_person_anchor.R` fitted the same model once on the real respondents, by maximum likelihood and with the respondents who named nothing scored zero, and @tbl-published shows its fixed part.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-published
#| tbl-cap: "The fixed part of the published model of OA without its cross-level interactions, on the cosmopolitan scale, fitted once on the real respondents with complete covariates, with random intercepts for countries and country-waves. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/anchor_person_fixed.csv`."
anchor_cosmo |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    estimate = insight::format_value(estimate, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus", zap_small = TRUE),
    se = insight::format_value(se, digits = 4, zap_small = TRUE),
    t = insight::format_value(t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c(term = "term", coefficient = "estimate",
                                     `standard error` = "se", t = "t")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

Among the national terms, a one-point rise in the unemployment rate of a country goes with a fall of about `r insight::format_value(abs(anchor_b[["munemp"]]), digits = 4)` in the cosmopolitan framing score of an individual, net of who that individual is. The term `sesunemployed` is the employment status of the respondent. Being unemployed rather than a manual worker moves the score by `r insight::format_value(anchor_b[["sesunemployed"]], digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`, roughly `r xfun::numbers_to_words(round(abs(anchor_b[["sesunemployed"]] / anchor_b[["munemp"]])))` times as much per unit, so individual circumstance matters far more to an individual than the national rate does.

The model of the paper differs from this one in a respect that matters for the coefficient that it prints. Its Model 1 also carries interactions of unemployment and of growth with education, so its unemployment coefficient, −0.00340 in Table 3 of the paper, is the slope for the low-education band, the reference category, rather than an average over the bands. The model above leaves the interactions out, and its slope is the average over the education bands. On the rebuilt respondents the version with the interactions gives a slope of `r insight::format_value(oa_published$b, digits = 5, style_negative = "minus")` for the low-education band (t = `r insight::format_value(oa_published$t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` on `r insight::format_value(oa_published$df_satterthwaite, digits = 1)` Satterthwaite degrees of freedom), and the version without them a slope of `r insight::format_value(oa_no_interactions$b, digits = 5, style_negative = "minus")` (t = `r insight::format_value(oa_no_interactions$t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` on `r insight::format_value(oa_no_interactions$df_satterthwaite, digits = 1)`). Both refits leave out the respondents who named nothing, as the code of OA did, where the fit above scores them zero, and that rule is why the second refit gives a steeper slope than the fit of @tbl-published. The multiverse chart places the original study by the second refit, tagged "OA design", at r = `r insight::format_value(oa_no_interactions$r_on_df, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`, so that its mark answers the same question as the five reanalyses. What the interactions themselves show, the education gap of the second hypothesis, is the subject of [section 10](#sec-claim2), which also shows what the rule for the respondents who named nothing does to it.

## 6. Individual effects and aggregate associations {#sec-composition}

The two coefficients of the previous section apply to different units, so they are not rival explanations of one thing. The individual effect applies to whoever is unemployed, and the contextual effect applies to everyone, in the sense of section 4: the coefficient on the national rate, in a model that holds the employment status of the respondent constant, is what Raudenbush and Bryk call a contextual effect. The question is how much of the association at the level of the country the individual effect could account for.

That depends on a quantity which neither coefficient contains, namely how much the unemployment rate of a country changes *who is in the sample*. Measured on the real respondents, a one-point rise in the published rate adds `r insight::format_value(grad$gradient[2], digits = 4)` to the share of respondents who are themselves unemployed, well under one percentage point.

```{r}
#| label: arithmetic
b_ind  <- anchor_b[["sesunemployed"]]
b_ctx  <- anchor_b[["munemp"]]
grad_w <- grad$gradient[2]

tibble::tibble(
  quantity = c("individual effect of being unemployed",
               "extra unemployed share per point of the national rate",
               "compositional contribution to the country-level slope",
               "the country-level slope itself",
               "compositional share of it"),
  value = c(b_ind, grad_w, b_ind * grad_w, b_ctx,
            b_ind * grad_w / b_ctx)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(value = signif(value, 3))
```

So the compositional path accounts for roughly `r insight::format_value(100 * b_ind * grad_w / b_ctx, digits = 1)`% of the association at the level of the country, because an effect several times the size, spread over a group that barely grows, moves the average hardly at all.

This calculation should be asked for whenever an aggregate association is explained by 'it must be the people who changed'. It is rarely done, and when it is done the compositional explanation usually does not hold up. It needs an individual-level effect *and* a prevalence gradient, meaning the amount by which the share of people in the group rises as the aggregate predictor rises, and the second is usually assumed, although it can be measured.

## 7. Two designs {#sec-designs}

The course panel and the model of OA are both defensible readings of the same claim, and they do not agree. Fitted with growth beside unemployment, as the paper fits it, the two-way design of the panel gives a smaller unemployment slope than the published design, and the reason lies in the years. The design of OA has random intercepts for countries and for country-waves but **no year effects**, the structure that @Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel call model D in their typology of random structures for comparative longitudinal survey data, and nothing in it removes a shock that hit every country at once. The year 2009 brought such a shock: unemployment rose everywhere and EU framing moved everywhere, for reasons that include but are not limited to unemployment. The two-way design removes that shock and the published design does not, so part of the shock ends up in the published estimate. Schmidt-Catran and Fairbrother recommend "to include random effects at all potentially relevant levels" (p. 23), years among them, and @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 124, n. 12] adds that "[i]f the number of years or waves is few, on the other hand, fixed effects will be more appropriate for controlling for such shocks". @tbl-designs sets the published design with the years added in both ways, fitted once on the real respondents by the script `fit_person_years.R`, beside the two-way design of the panel.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-designs
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("The unemployment coefficient under the designs of the panel and of OA, with t in brackets, on the cosmopolitan and the libertarian scales. The panel row is the two-way fixed-effects regression of the 270 cell means with growth as an adjustment, with conventional t; the other rows are the published design without its interactions, with Satterthwaite t, fitted once on the ", n_complete, " real respondents with complete covariates. Source of the rows of the respondents: `companion/_model-outputs/person_year_effects.csv`.")'
agg_cosmo <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + growth + factor(year) + factor(cntry), data = panel)
agg_lib <- lm(mlib ~ unemp + growth + factor(year) + factor(cntry), data = panel)

all_designs <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(outcome = c("cosmo", "lib"), design = "two_way", source = "panel",
                 estimate = c(coef(agg_cosmo)[["unemp"]], coef(agg_lib)[["unemp"]]),
                 t = c(summary(agg_cosmo)$coefficients["unemp", "t value"],
                       summary(agg_lib)$coefficients["unemp", "t value"])),
  years_real |>
    datawizard::data_filter(kind == "fixed", term == "munemp") |>
    datawizard::data_select(select = c("outcome", "design", "estimate", "t")) |>
    datawizard::data_modify(source = "respondents")
)

all_designs |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = paste0(insight::format_value(estimate, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus", zap_small = TRUE),
                               " (", insight::format_value(t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"), ")"),
                design = factor(design, levels = c("two_way", "published", "year_random", "year_dummy")),
                source = factor(source, levels = c("panel", "respondents"))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("design", "source")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Design = c(two_way = "Two-way fixed effects",
               published = "Published: random intercepts for countries and country-years",
               year_random = "Published, with random intercepts for years",
               year_dummy = "Published, with a dummy for each year")[as.character(design)],
    Data = c(panel = "panel", respondents = "real respondents")[as.character(source)],
    outcome, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = value) |>
  datawizard::data_rename(select = c("cosmo", "lib"), replacement = c("Cosmopolitan", "Libertarian")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:4, align = "r")
```

```{r}
#| label: designs-values
#| include: false
dv_of <- all_designs |> datawizard::data_modify(key = paste(outcome, design, source, sep = "_"))
dval <- stats::setNames(dv_of$estimate, dv_of$key)
dt <- stats::setNames(dv_of$t, dv_of$key)
```

The published design gives `r insight::format_value(dval[["cosmo_published_respondents"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` on the real respondents, against `r insight::format_value(dval[["cosmo_two_way_panel"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` for the two-way design of the panel. The script declares the 270 country-years, rather than the `r oa_no_interactions$country_waves` country-waves of the paper, as the middle level of the design, which is why its slope differs from the `r insight::format_value(anchor_b[["munemp"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` of @tbl-published. A random intercept for each year moves the published estimate to `r insight::format_value(dval[["cosmo_year_random_respondents"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` on the real respondents (t = `r insight::format_value(dt[["cosmo_year_random_respondents"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`), and a dummy for each year to `r insight::format_value(dval[["cosmo_year_dummy_respondents"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")`, both close to the slope of the panel. Neither estimate is wrong, because the two designs address different questions, which is the central argument of the course applied at the individual level, and the difference between them is larger than the difference made by most of the choices on the specification menu. On the libertarian scale the disagreement between the designs is starker. The published design finds a clear association, `r insight::format_value(dval[["lib_published_respondents"]], digits = 4, style_positive = "plus")` with t = `r insight::format_value(dt[["lib_published_respondents"]], digits = 2)` on the real respondents, while the panel finds almost none (`r insight::format_value(dval[["lib_two_way_panel"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus", style_positive = "plus")`), and a term for the years removes the association from the respondents as well (`r insight::format_value(dval[["lib_year_random_respondents"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus", style_positive = "plus")` with random intercepts for years, t = `r insight::format_value(dt[["lib_year_random_respondents"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`). When an effect appears under one defensible design and not under another, that is a strong argument for fixing the design in a preregistration before any model is fitted.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

In the workspace, fit the published model of section 5 again with `ses` removed and note what happens to `munemp`. It should barely move, and the reason is section 6: the compositional path is a few per cent of the total, so deleting the variable through which it runs changes little. Then remove the random intercept for country-waves, `(1 | cntry:eb)`, and compare the degrees of freedom of `munemp` with those of the full model, which repeats on the published model the lesson of section 3.

Finally, take the decomposition of section 4 to the respondents, as Fairbrother proposes. Join the mean unemployment of each country over the decade to `person`, for example from `datawizard::demean(panel, select = "unemp", by = "cntry")` on the course panel that `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` reads in as `panel`, replace `munemp` by the country mean and the departure from it, add `(1 | year)`, and set the slope of the departure beside the two-way slope of the panel.
:::

## 8. Weights {#sec-weights}

```{r}
#| label: weights-values
#| include: false
# the panel of weights and the files of the curve and of its deviations, which
# only this section reads
pw <- datawizard::data_read("../data/teney_panel_weights.csv", verbose = FALSE)
cy <- datawizard::data_read("../data/europeanisation_cy.csv", verbose = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
devs <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "weights")
dev_rows <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "weights")
# percentages round halves up, as the specification menu does; pct() takes a
# proportion and pc() a value already in per cent
pc <- \(x) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^1 + 0.5) / 10^1, format = "f", digits = 1), "%")
pct <- \(x) pc(100 * x)
pc_small <- \(x) if (x < 0.1) "less than 0.1%" else pc(x)
num <- \(x, d = 3) gsub("-", "−", formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f"), fixed = TRUE)
sig <- \(x) gsub("-", "−", formatC(x, format = "g", digits = 3), fixed = TRUE)
fk <- \(ax, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == ax]
dv <- \(op, col) devs[[col]][devs$option == op]
below_sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports & d$sig)

# the reproduced specification and its twin with design-weighted cells, as they
# stand on the curve, and the same two under each regression weight
ref_spec <- \(d) d |>
  dplyr::filter(outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "unemp", copredictor == "none",
         estimator == "fe_twoway", noop == "zero", item_set == "all",
         measure == "wb_nat", pred_form == "raw")
c6hjr <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  curve |> ref_spec() |>
    dplyr::transmute(cell_weight, reg_weight = "none", b, t = t_cr2, df = df_cr2, p = p_cr2, r = r_ca),
  dev_rows |> ref_spec() |>
    dplyr::transmute(cell_weight, reg_weight = option, b = b_dev, t = t_dev, df = df_dev, p = p_dev, r = r_ca_dev)
)
cw <- \(cell, reg, col) c6hjr[[col]][c6hjr$cell_weight == cell & c6hjr$reg_weight == reg]
```

Every Eurobarometer respondent arrives with a post-stratification weight, W1, which the models of the respondents above have so far ignored. In this case study weights enter at two levels, inside each country-year and across the country-years, and the specification menu has a decision at each: the **cell weighting** decides, with two options, how the respondents of a country-year are averaged, and the decision **whose average** decides, with four, how much each country-year counts in the regression. Between them the two decisions cover three different questions, which are settled at two different levels of the analysis and are justified by different arguments, and only one of the three changes what the analysis is estimating.

| | Level | The argument for it | Does it change the estimand? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Survey weighting** | inside a country-year cell | The achieved sample is not a miniature of the country, so weight the respondents before averaging them | No. It makes the cell mean a better estimate of the same quantity |
| **Precision weighting** | across cells | A cell mean built on more interviews is measured more precisely, so let it count for more | No. It is an efficiency argument about estimating the same slope |
| **Population weighting** | across cells | The claim is about Europeans, not about countries, so a country should count in proportion to how many people live in it | **Yes.** The slope now describes a different average |

: The three decisions that are grouped under the word 'weight' in this analysis. {#tbl-three}

The first is a *measurement* decision, because it changes how well the number in the cell estimates the thing it names. The second is a decision about *the model*, which changes the efficiency of the fit and leaves the target alone. The third is a decision about *the question*: it changes whose average the coefficient describes, and two analysts who resolve it differently are answering different questions. When all three go under the one word 'weighting', a change of question can be reported as though it were a technical robustness check. The curve of the claim keeps the unweighted regression and both ways of building the cell means, and this section gives the reasons. What a survey weight is, the strata and clusters of a survey design and the standard errors that follow such a design are taught in full by the module on [weights and survey design](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-cohabitation/companion/weighting.html) of the Cohabitation and marriage case study.

### The weights of the Eurobarometer {#sec-weights-eurobarometer}

The weighting scheme of the Eurobarometer is documented in the weighting overview of the GESIS Eurobarometer Data Service [@GESISWeightingOverview], and the data file for every wave labels its weights plainly. The basic one is **W1, "WEIGHT RESULT FROM TARGET"**, which is the variable `w1` in the rebuilt person file. It is a pure post-stratification weight (*redressment*, in the vocabulary of the Eurobarometer). An iterative procedure adjusts the weights to one margin after another until each national sample matches the known distribution of its population by sex, age, region (NUTS 2) and size of locality, while keeping the real number of cases in each country. W1 makes each national sample representative *of its own country*, and it does not rescale countries against one another. GESIS supplies no design weight for the unequal chances of selection that depend on the size of a household, as the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-eurobarometer) quotes from its documentation.

Of the other weights in the file, W3 ("WEIGHT GERMANY") and W4 ("WEIGHT UNITED KINGDOM") combine the separately drawn East/West German and Great Britain/Northern Ireland samples into united national totals, the same splits that are merged by the DE and GB recodes in the course codebook. The long W5–W30 series ("WEIGHT EU6" through "WEIGHT EU27", euro zone in and out) add the population-size scaling needed when similarly sized national samples must stand for populations as different as those of Malta and Germany, and **WEX** ("WEIGHT EXTRA POPULATION 15+") extrapolates results to the actual population aged fifteen and over. For a question about the within-country association between framing and unemployment, W1 is the natural choice, and it is the natural weight to offer in any person-level universe of specifications built from this menu.

::: {.callout-important title="Choosing among Eurobarometer weights"}
A Eurobarometer file contains several weight variables, and they are not interchangeable. Choosing the wrong one changes the question being answered, and no warning appears in the output. Using a European weight and then averaging countries double-counts population size; using a national weight and then pooling respondents across countries gives you an average over *respondents*, which is an artefact of how many interviews each country happened to get. Whenever a survey provides more than one weight, read the codebook before choosing, because the choice among them is, in effect, the choice between a country-level and a person-level estimand.
:::

No model of OA uses a weight, as the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-selection) notes from the code of the paper. Of the five analysts of the robustness study, KQXUE and 018OL averaged the respondents of each cell without weights. In the code of KQXUE two lines settle the whole weighting question by default:

```stata
collapse cosmo util, by(cntry year)    // unweighted country-year means
xtreg cosmo unemployment, fe           // = the within estimator of section 4 of Panel data
```

The `collapse` command averages every respondent equally, so the survey weights are gone before any model is fitted, and each cell then counts equally in `xtreg` whether 300 people or 3,000 stand behind it. That is the choice which the `n_cell` option of the menu, set out below, switches on and off. (For Stata users: `xtreg, fe` after `xtset cntry_num year` is the within estimator of `plm` in R.)

### Weights within the cells {#sec-weights-cells}

Applying W1 changes the country-year means by a small but not negligible amount. Across the `r nrow(pw)` cells, the largest change to the cosmopolitan scale is `r sig(max(abs(pw$w_mcosmo - cy$mcosmo[match(paste(pw$cntry, pw$year), paste(cy$cntry, cy$year))])))` on a 0–1 scale whose mean is about 0.51, and the weighted and unweighted cell means correlate at `r round(cor(pw$w_mcosmo, cy$mcosmo[match(paste(pw$cntry, pw$year), paste(cy$cntry, cy$year))]), 4)`. Because the two versions move together, the choice almost never changes a result. On the curve of the claim the cell weighting carries `r pc_small(fk("cell_weight"))` of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation, and moving it alone changes whether a specification lies below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 in `r pc(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs. Both options stay on the curve, the design-weighted mean as the better estimator of a national quantity in principle, and the mean of the respondents as interviewed because it is the one that the original study and the course panel use.

Weighting improves representativeness at a cost in precision. When respondents have unequal weights, the weighted mean is less precise than an unweighted mean of the same number of interviews, because a few heavily weighted cases contribute a disproportionate share of the estimate. Kish's **effective sample size**, the number of interviews divided by the design effect of the weights, is the standard way of saying how much precision is left:

$$n_\text{eff} = \frac{\left(\sum_i w_i\right)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2}$$

For a cell where every weight is equal, $n_\text{eff} = n$. As the weights spread out, it falls. In this panel the median cell has $n = `r median(pw$n_cy)`$ interviews and $n_\text{eff} = `r round(median(pw$n_eff))`$, a design effect (the ratio of $n$ to $n_\text{eff}$) of `r round(median(pw$deff), 2)`; the worst cell loses `r pct(1 - 1 / max(pw$deff))` of its sample to the weighting. The practical consequence is that if you are going to weight cells by their precision, $n_\text{eff}$ is the right variable and $n$ is an approximation to it.

### Weights across the cells {#sec-weights-across}

Once you have `r nrow(pw)` country-year means, you have to decide how much each one counts in the regression. There are four candidate answers, and each makes a different claim.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-candidates
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The four regression weights on the menu."
tinytable::tt(
  tibble::tibble(
    Setting = c("`none`", "`n_cell`", "`n_eff`", "`pop`"),
    `What it weights by` = c("nothing; every cell counts once",
      "respondents interviewed", "effective sample size",
      "adult population of the country that year"),
    `The claim it makes` = c(
      "The claim is about countries. Malta and Germany are two observations",
      "Cells measured on more interviews are more reliable evidence",
      "The same argument, using the precision that the weighting actually leaves",
      "The claim is about Europeans. A German counts as much as a Maltese"),
    Kind = c("estimand: the average country", "precision", "precision",
             "estimand: the average European"))) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

The precision weights rest on an assumption about why the cell means scatter around the fitted line. If they scattered mainly because each is measured with sampling error, the cells built on more interviews would be the more reliable evidence, and weighting by their sample size would estimate the same slope more efficiently. On these data the assumption fails. Across the 270 cells the sampling variance of a cell mean of the cosmopolitan share averages 0.000103, against a residual variance of 0.00141 in the reproduced model, so that about 7% of the variation that the model leaves unexplained is sampling noise, and the rest is genuine variation between country-years that a larger sample would not have reduced. Under those conditions efficient weights are close to equal. Weights that run from `r format(min(pw$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(pw$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents therefore buy little precision, and what they mostly do is shift weight towards the years in which two survey waves were fielded and towards the countries with the largest samples.

It is tempting to treat the respondent count (`n_cy` in the panel, `n_cell` on the menu) as a size variable, on the reasoning that bigger countries get bigger samples. They do not, or not by much. Eurobarometer fields roughly a thousand interviews in each member state whatever its size, with smaller allocations for the smallest states and a larger one for Germany. So across this panel:

- the respondent count runs from `r min(pw$n_cy)` to `r max(pw$n_cy)`, a ratio of **`r round(max(pw$n_cy) / min(pw$n_cy), 1)` to 1**;
- the adult population runs from `r format(min(pw$pop_15plus), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(pw$pop_15plus), big.mark = ",")`, a ratio of **`r round(max(pw$pop_15plus) / min(pw$pop_15plus))` to 1**;
- and the two correlate at only `r round(cor(pw$n_cy, pw$pop_15plus), 2)` across the `r nrow(pw)` cells.

Weighting by `n_cell` therefore does *not* make the analysis representative of the European population. It gives better-measured cells more say in the fit, which is a different and much weaker claim. If you want the average European, you have to weight by population and state that you have done so.

@tbl-c6hjr shows the reproduced specification (cosmopolitan framing on raw World Bank unemployment, two-way fixed effects, all years, no adjustment, respondents who mention nothing scored zero) fitted under all eight combinations of the two ways of building the cell means and the four regression weights.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-c6hjr
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The reproduced specification under every weighting choice. The first two rows stand on the curve of the claim; the first is the reproduced C6HJR result. The t is the coefficient divided by its CR2 standard error, clustered by country, df are its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and p is the CR2 p-value that classes the curve. Sources: `data/spec_curve.csv` and `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz`."
tinytable::tt(
  c6hjr |>
    dplyr::arrange(factor(reg_weight, c("none", "n_cell", "n_eff", "pop")),
            factor(cell_weight, c("unweighted", "design"))) |>
    dplyr::transmute(`Cell mean` = dplyr::if_else(cell_weight == "design", "design-weighted", "as interviewed"),
              `Regression weight` = reg_weight,
              b = num(b, 5), `CR2 t` = num(t, 2), df = num(df, 1), `CR2 p` = num(p), r = num(r, 3))) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:7, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

Every row lies below zero, so no weighting choice reverses the direction of the association, but its strength and the verdict on it change. The partial correlation runs from `r num(max(c6hjr$r), 3)` to `r num(min(c6hjr$r), 3)` across eight versions of a specification that any methods section would describe in the same sentence, and the two kinds of weight pull in **opposite directions**. Precision weighting by the respondent count weakens the result, from a CR2 t of `r num(cw("unweighted", "none", "t"), 2)` to `r num(cw("unweighted", "n_cell", "t"), 2)` and from a p of `r num(cw("unweighted", "none", "p"))` to `r num(cw("unweighted", "n_cell", "p"))`. Population weighting strengthens the coefficient against its standard error, to t = `r num(cw("unweighted", "pop", "t"), 2)`, but the test becomes no more decisive, with p = `r num(cw("unweighted", "pop", "p"))`, because the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom fall from `r num(cw("unweighted", "none", "df"), 1)` to `r num(cw("unweighted", "pop", "df"), 1)`. A weight in proportion to population hands most of the information to the few largest countries, and the degrees of freedom count how few of them are left carrying it. An analyst who reasons "I should weight, because weighting is more careful" without saying which argument they are making could end up with either.

Kish's correction changes almost nothing. With cells as interviewed, `n_eff` and `n_cell` are the same weight, because a cell mean that uses no survey weights has an effective sample size equal to its number of respondents, and with design-weighted cells they give CR2 t values of `r num(cw("design", "n_eff", "t"), 2)` and `r num(cw("design", "n_cell", "t"), 2)`. $n_\text{eff}$ is the correct precision weight, but the design effects in this panel are small enough that choosing it over `n_cell` does not change the conclusion.

The same holds across the curve. Swapped into every one of its `r nrow(curve)` specifications, the respondent weight leaves `r pc(dv("n_cell", "below_zero_sig"))` of them below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 and the effective sample size `r pc(dv("n_eff", "below_zero_sig"))`, against `r pc(below_sig(curve))` on the curve itself, and each changes the class of `r pc(dv("n_cell", "class_changes"))` of the pairs. The curve keeps only the unweighted fit, because the precision weights rest on an argument that the error structure of these data does not support, and the population weight, which the next subsection takes up, answers another question.

### The average European {#sec-average-european}

Weighting by adult population changes the quantity to the average European, in which the largest member state counts `r round(max(pw$pop_15plus) / min(pw$pop_15plus))` times as much as the smallest. That is a defensible estimand, the one that a reader interested in the climate of opinion in the Union as a whole would want, but it is not the estimand of the claim. The claim concerns how a national economy shapes the framing of its citizens, so its unit is the member state, and the unweighted fit, in which Malta counts as much as Germany, is what a claim about national economies asks for. A result about the average European can therefore neither confirm nor undermine a result about the average member state, and it belongs in an analysis with its own estimand statement rather than among the robustness checks of the claim.

Across the curve the population weight leaves `r pc(dv("pop", "below_zero"))` of the specifications below zero, slightly more than the curve itself, but only `r pc(dv("pop", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, and it changes the class of `r pc(dv("pop", "class_changes"))` of the pairs. The fall in significance most probably reflects the weight itself, which lets a few large countries dominate the fit and leaves fewer countries to carry the evidence, while at the reproduced specification, as @tbl-c6hjr shows, the same weight strengthens the result. The two estimands diverge in ways that a single specification does not reveal, which is a further reason for reporting the population-weighted analysis on its own terms.

### The denominator {#sec-denominator}

When asked what the EU means to them, `r format(sum(pw$n_noop), big.mark = ",")` respondents, `r pct(sum(pw$n_noop) / sum(pw$n_cy))` of the sample, mentioned nothing at all, and how they are scored is a decision that no weight can change. The course panel follows the reanalyst C6HJR in scoring them **0** on all four framing scales, so that a person with no opinion enters the data as a person with no cosmopolitan framing, while the code of the original paper dropped those respondents; the section [Respondents who mention nothing](measurement.qmd#sec-noop) of the module on scale construction sets out what each rule assumes and which analysts took it.

Scoring the silent respondents zero would be a defensible convention if the no-opinion rate were the same everywhere, but the rate differs widely between countries, as the [table of the four highest and four lowest rates](measurement.qmd#tbl-noop-countries) in that section shows. An eight-fold difference in the rate of a response coded as a substantive zero is a measurement problem that no weight will fix, since the weights correct the composition of the respondents and leave the scoring of their answers untouched. Whether the silent respondents are dropped or scored zero belongs with the measurement decisions of the [specification menu](../menu.qmd), and the curve keeps both rules.

### Weights in models of the respondents {#sec-weights-respondents}

The models of the respondents can carry W1 as well. In R, design-based estimation is the job of the survey package [@Lumley2004AnalysisComplexSurvey]. You declare the design once – weights and, where the data supply them, clusters and strata – and then every estimator in the package takes it into account, as [section 3 of the Cohabitation module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-cohabitation/companion/weighting.html#sec-design) shows for a survey that supplies all three. The rebuilt person file holds no identifiers of the primary sampling units, so the design here declares the weights alone:

```{r}
#| label: code-svyglm
#| eval: false
des <- survey::svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~w1, data = person)   # weights only; the file has no primary sampling unit (PSU) ids
m_svy <- survey::svyglm(s_cosmo ~ unemp, design = des)
summary(m_svy)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-svyglm
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "svyglm.txt")))
```

The W1-weighted pooled slope is +0.0001 with t = 0.8, which is no association at all, and its sign is the opposite of the one that the claim predicts. The weights have corrected the *representation* of the sample, but they cannot correct a mis-specified model, and this is the pooled estimator of [section 3 of Panel data](panel-data.qmd#sec-pooled) again, blending within-country and between-country variation across 27 countries. The output also shows that `svyglm()` reports design-robust (linearised) standard errors by default.

A weighted multilevel model is a harder problem, because it needs a weight at each level, the country and then the respondent within the country, while surveys publish one all-in weight per person. The standard answer, **pseudo-maximum-likelihood**, weights the contribution of each level to the likelihood [@Rabe-HeskethSkrondal2006MultilevelModellingComplex] and leaves open how the weights of the lower level are scaled, a choice that can move the variance estimates noticeably [@Carle2009FittingMultilevelModels], as [section 9 of the Cohabitation module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-cohabitation/companion/weighting.html#sec-other-models) explains. Because implementations differ in those choices, **the same weighted multilevel model can return different numbers in different software**, and knowing which convention you are running is part of reporting the model.

The `weights` argument of `lmer()` is *not* a survey-weights argument. It treats weights as precision weights, a different quantity entirely, and if you pass it `w1` it returns answers that are inconsistent with the sample design, without any warning. The `mixed` command in Stata accepts probability weights (`[pw = ...]`) and implements pseudo-maximum-likelihood with its own scaling options (`pwscale()`), and the R package that follows the conventions of Stata is **WeMix** [@BaileyEtAl2023WeMixWeightedMixed], which takes one weight column per level. In our own comparative survey work it has reproduced to three decimals the coefficients of the fixed part of weighted `mixed` models in Stata, which makes it the tool of choice when a published Stata result needs re-implementing in R.

On the data of this case study, the two-level model of [section 3](#sec-levels) fitted with WeMix, with the W1 weights at the respondent level and a constant weight of 1 at the country level, reproduces the common 'weights at level 1 only' scenario:

```{r}
#| label: code-wemix
#| eval: false
person <- person |>
  datawizard::data_modify(w_lvl2 = 1)   # unit weight at the country level – weighting at level 1 only
m_wemix <- WeMix::mix(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry), data = person,
                      weights = c("w1", "w_lvl2"))
summary(m_wemix)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-wemix
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "wemix_2lvl.txt")))
```

Compare this with the unweighted two-level fit of [section 3](#sec-levels), and read the comparison carefully, because the two fits differ in more than the weights. The weighted slope, −0.0049, is almost the same as the unweighted −0.0048, so the W1 weights barely move the estimate, and the association between framing and unemployment is not an artefact of who is over- or under-represented within national samples. The standard errors, though, are 0.0015 here against 0.0002 there, and they are not comparable at a glance. Most of that gap comes from the *variance estimator*, since WeMix reports design-linearised (robust) standard errors while `lmer()` reports model-based ones, so two settings changed between the outputs and only one of them is the weighting. The rule of the specification menu, one decision at a time, applies here too: before attributing a difference to the weights, make sure that every other setting, the variance estimator included, is the same in both fits.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

1. Pick any specification from the curve (`data/spec_curve.csv`) and look up its twins under the three regression weights in `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz` (`axis == "weights"`). Write one sentence per weight, the unweighted fit included, stating what the coefficient is the average *of*.
2. Three of those four sentences describe the same quantity, and two of them give the same number. Which, and why?
3. The `no_bailout` sample and the `pop` weight both change the population that the claim is about, and neither stands on the curve of the claim. One of them is conventionally reported as a robustness check and the other as a modelling choice. Should either be?
:::

## 9. Bounded outcomes {#sec-glm}

```{r}
#| label: glm-values
#| include: false
# values read from the saved outputs of fit_models.R, which ran on the
# licensed respondent file; each row is split into its printed columns
cosmo_dist <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/cosmo_dist.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
logit_row <- readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "glm_logit.txt")) |>
  grep(pattern = "^unemp ", value = TRUE) |>
  trimws() |>
  strsplit("\\s+") |>
  unlist()
ordbeta_lines <- readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "glmmtmb_ordbeta.txt"))
ordbeta_row <- ordbeta_lines |>
  grep(pattern = "^unemp ", value = TRUE) |>
  trimws() |>
  strsplit("\\s+") |>
  unlist()
ordbeta_phi <- ordbeta_lines |>
  grep(pattern = "^Dispersion parameter", value = TRUE) |>
  sub(pattern = ".*: ", replacement = "") |>
  as.numeric()

# the reproduced specification of the panel and its twin in the beta family
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref <- curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
devs <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
beta_dev <- devs |> datawizard::data_filter(axis == "family", option == "beta")
cr1_dev <- devs |> datawizard::data_filter(axis == "se", option == "cr1_g1")
beta_ref <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", option == "beta",
                          outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "unemp", copredictor == "none",
                          estimator == "fe_twoway", noop == "zero", item_set == "all",
                          cell_weight == "unweighted", measure == "wb_nat", pred_form == "raw")
```

One assumption has gone unexamined in every model so far: that a Gaussian linear model is the right shape for this outcome. Strictly, it never was. Every framing scale in this case study is bounded between 0 and 1, whereas a Gaussian model has unbounded support, so a straight line extended far enough always predicts impossible values, and nothing inside `lm()` or `lmer()` takes the bounds into account. The assumption is wrong at both levels of the data. What differs between the levels is how much that matters, as the two panels of @fig-outcome-scales show.

```{r}
#| label: fig-outcome-scales
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "The same outcome at two levels. Left: the cosmopolitan score of the respondents is bounded, with heavy masses at exactly 0 and exactly 1, a shape that no Gaussian can imitate. Right: averaging within country-years produces 270 cell means bunched in the middle of the scale, far from either bound, where a Gaussian model is a safe working approximation despite being wrong in principle. The distribution of the respondents is plotted from committed aggregate counts (`companion/_model-outputs/cosmo_dist.csv`)."
#| code-fold: true
p_person <- ggplot2::ggplot(cosmo_dist, ggplot2::aes(cosmo, n_respondents / sum(n_respondents))) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.022, fill = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.02, 1.02)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = paste(format(sum(cosmo_dist$n_respondents), big.mark = ","), "respondents"),
                x = "cosmopolitan framing score",
                y = "share of respondents") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
p_cells <- ggplot2::ggplot(panel, ggplot2::aes(mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, boundary = 0, fill = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "270 country-year means", x = "mean cosmopolitan framing",
                y = "count of cells") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_person, p_cells)
```

At the level of the country-year (right panel) the cell means bunch in the middle of the scale, several residual standard deviations clear of either bound. Fitted values from the models of the panel module never approach the bounds, the probability that the Gaussian error places beyond them is negligible, and the approximation is safe *in practice*, because of where this particular outcome happens to lie and not because the model allows for the bounds. That is a judgement to make consciously, and to make again whenever an outcome drifts towards its floor or ceiling. At the level of the respondent (left panel) the judgement goes the other way. The score of a respondent is the share of the mentioned items that are cosmopolitan, `r insight::format_value(100 * cosmo_dist$n_respondents[cosmo_dist$cosmo == 0] / sum(cosmo_dist$n_respondents), digits = 0)`% of all respondents sit at exactly 0 and another `r insight::format_value(100 * cosmo_dist$n_respondents[cosmo_dist$cosmo == 1] / sum(cosmo_dist$n_respondents), digits = 0)`% at exactly 1, and a Gaussian model treats those masses as ordinary noise around a middle that describes almost nobody.

The family of **generalised linear models** (GLMs) fixes the shape problem by modelling a *transformed* mean,

$$ g\!\left( \mathbb{E}[y_i] \right) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i $$

in which the **linear predictor** $\eta_i$ stays a familiar straight line, the **link function** $g$ maps the constrained mean of the outcome onto the unconstrained line, and a distribution suited to the values that the outcome can take replaces the Gaussian. The classic member is **logistic regression**, for binary outcomes, with the log-odds link, here for the outcome collapsed to 'mentions at least one cosmopolitan item':

$$ \log \frac{p_i}{1 - p_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \qquad p_i = \Pr(y_i = 1) $$

```{r}
#| label: code-logit
#| eval: false
m_logit <- glm(I(s_cosmo > 0) ~ unemp, family = binomial(), data = person)
summary(m_logit)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-logit
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "glm_logit.txt")))
```

Reading the coefficients of a GLM takes one extra step, because the estimate is on the scale of the link. The slope of `r insight::format_value(as.numeric(logit_row[2]), digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")` is a change in *log-odds* for each point of unemployment, exponentiating gives an odds ratio of $e^{`r insight::format_value(as.numeric(logit_row[2]), digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`} \approx `r insight::format_value(exp(as.numeric(logit_row[2])), digits = 3)`$, and the 'divide by 4 rule' of @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing [p. 82] bounds the change in probability at about `r insight::format_value(100 * as.numeric(logit_row[2]) / 4, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` percentage points for each point of unemployment. The `z value` replaces `t`, because the dispersion is fixed rather than estimated, and the **deviance** replaces R-squared as the measure of fit. The z of `r insight::format_value(as.numeric(logit_row[4]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` should now look suspicious, for the reason given in section 3: it comes from treating the `r n_resp` respondents as if each were fresh evidence about 270 unemployment values. The generalised and the multilevel extensions deal with separate problems, and this outcome needs both at once.

For a *bounded continuous* outcome the classical tool is **beta regression**, which models a variable on the open interval (0, 1) with a mean linked by the logit and a precision parameter $\phi$. For this variable its defect is the masses at the endpoints, because the beta distribution places no probability at exactly 0 or 1, and the traditional workaround, nudging the data inward, is the kind of silent choice that this course sets out to make visible. **Ordered beta regression** [@Kubinec2023OrderedBetaRegression] builds the endpoints into the model. A single model uses ordered cutpoints to decide whether an observation is exactly 0, in between, or exactly 1, with a beta distribution for the middle, and one vector of coefficients governs all three parts, so that the slope keeps a single interpretation.

Both inferential traditions, frequentist and Bayesian, implement it. The frequentist route is **glmmTMB** [@BrooksEtAl2017GlmmTMBBalancesSpeed], a fast engine of maximum likelihood for GLMs with random effects, here with the full three-level structure of section 3, on all `r n_resp` respondents:

```{r}
#| label: code-ordbeta
#| eval: false
m_ordfreq <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year),
                              family = glmmTMB::ordbeta(), data = person)
summary(m_ordfreq)
```

```{r}
#| label: out-ordbeta
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines(file.path("_model-outputs", "glmmtmb_ordbeta.txt")))
```

The output is made of pieces that you now recognise: variance components for the two grouping levels (on the latent logit scale, so not directly comparable with those of section 3), a dispersion parameter ($\phi$ = `r insight::format_value(ordbeta_phi, digits = 2)`, the precision of the beta part), and a slope of `r insight::format_value(as.numeric(ordbeta_row[2]), digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")` in the conditional model on the logit scale, with z = `r insight::format_value(as.numeric(ordbeta_row[4]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`. The same rule of Gelman and Hill translates that slope to at most `r insight::format_value(100 * as.numeric(ordbeta_row[2]) / 4, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` percentage points of cosmopolitan share for each point of unemployment, the same order as every Gaussian estimate of it, now from a model whose predictions cannot leave the unit interval. The z is far smaller in magnitude than in the bare logistic model, because the random effects do the work of clustering that the bare model ignored.

The Bayesian route is **ordbetareg**, the implementation of the model by Kubinec on top of brms [@Kubinec2023OrderedBetaRegression], and the [module on Bayesian estimation](bayesian.qmd#sec-bayes) explains how the output of such a fit is read.

On the country-year panel the beta family is a check of functional form rather than a repair. The cell means lie strictly inside the unit interval, as the right panel above showed, so a plain beta regression with the logit link is well defined there, with the fixed effects entered as country and year dummies, and the bounds matter most for the utilitarian scale, whose cell means come down to `r insight::format_value(min(panel$mutil), digits = 2)`. Its slope is on the logit scale, and its z statistic is converted to a partial correlation on the residual degrees of freedom of the fit, as the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-onescale) describes: at the reproduced specification the slope is `r insight::format_value(beta_ref$b_dev, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")`, with a claim-aligned partial correlation of `r insight::format_value(beta_ref$r_ca_dev, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")` against `r insight::format_value(ref$r_ca, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")` for the linear fit, and swapped into every specification of the curve the beta family puts `r insight::format_value(beta_dev$below_zero, digits = 1)`% of the fits below zero, as many as the linear family does, and moves the partial correlation by a median of `r insight::format_value(beta_dev$median_shift, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`.
