The family stays off the curve for a reason of inference rather than of fit: the clubSandwich package, which computes the CR2 test of the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference), does not cover beta regression, so the beta fits can only be tested by errors clustered by country on G − 1 degrees of freedom, under which `r insight::format_value(beta_dev$below_zero_sig, digits = 1)`% of the beta twins lie below zero with p < 0.05, against `r insight::format_value(cr1_dev$below_zero_sig, digits = 1)`% of the linear specifications under the same rule. Keeping both families would double the number of points on the curve without adding an answer while putting two rules of significance on one chart, and the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimation) records the option among the decisions about the model.

At the level of the respondent the beta likelihood is unavailable, because the scales of the respondents place real mass on exact zeros and ones, and the ordered beta model above, or a fractional-response binomial model with the logit link, takes its place. The general point holds at both levels. A family of models is one more fork, and because a universe of specifications grows geometrically one defensible fork at a time, the discipline is to state in advance which forks you consider defensible and why, which is the job of a preregistration, rather than to run the largest universe that you can afford.

## 10. The education gap {#sec-claim2}

The second hypothesis of the paper is about people inside countries, and it cannot be tested on the 270-row panel at all. The abstract states the finding in one sentence, which serves as the claim card for a second replication exercise in the style of the first:

> "…high unemployment rates affect the EU framing of high-educated citizens to a larger extent…" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619], or, in other words from the same abstract, "high unemployment rates are associated with a smaller gap between high- and low-educated citizens in the way they frame the EU".

> **Unemployment × high education → cosmopolitan EU framing: b = −0.0031, t = −6.93, p < .001** (Table 3, Model 1), beside an education gap of b = 0.0771 (t = 41.79) and an unemployment slope of b = −0.0034 (t = −4.03) at the lowest education band.

The estimand statement, in the form that the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#the-estimand-statement) uses, reads: among respondents in the 27 member states surveyed between 2004 and 2013, the difference between high- and low-educated respondents in the association between the national unemployment rate, measured as the World Bank series, and cosmopolitan EU framing, built as the share of the mentions of a respondent, comparing each country with itself over time. The quantity is an interaction, the amount by which the association with unemployment differs between education bands, and that is what makes the claim one about individuals. Education is a property of respondents and unemployment a property of country-years, and the question is whether people who differ on the first respond differently to the second. Multilevel modellers call such a term a **cross-level interaction**, which @HeisigSchaeffer2019WhyYouShould [p. 258] describe as "a specific type of context effect that may be understood as an upper-level variable moderating the association between a lower-level predictor and the outcome".

**Three ways to estimate it.** The published model is a three-level random-intercept model with the interaction terms and the full set of covariates, fitted on the respondents. The same interaction can be fitted with country and year fixed effects instead of random intercepts. Those effects remove the average level of framing in each country and the shocks common to all countries in a year. They do not absorb the national unemployment rate, which moves within each country from one year to the next, so both its slope and the difference of that slope between bands remain estimable. Because the three bands of a country share one country effect, the difference between bands draws on differences between countries in the size of the education gap as well as on movement within each country. And the interaction can be fitted on cells rather than respondents. The [panel by education band](../data/europeanisation_cy_edu_codebook.md) holds one row for each country, year and band, and a fixed-effects regression on its 810 rows, weighted by the respondents behind each mean, addresses the same question with the same data at the aggregate level. The first two were run on the real respondents, and the third runs here, on public data, in a few lines:

```{r}
#| label: claim2-cells
m_edu <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ edu3 * munemp + edu3 * mgrowth | cntry + year,
                       data = edu, weights = ~n, vcov = ~cntry)
parameters::model_parameters(m_edu, keep = "edu3|munemp") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "t", "p")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(Coefficient, SE),
                              \(x) insight::format_value(x, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus", zap_small = TRUE)),
                t = insight::format_value(t, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"),
                p = insight::format_p(p, stars = FALSE, name = NULL, digits = 3)) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-claim2
#| tbl-cap: "The education gap and its interaction with unemployment on the cosmopolitan scale, under three designs and two rules for the respondents who named nothing. The published model is fitted on the real respondents with the covariates of OA and random intercepts for countries and country-waves; the fixed-effects model on the same respondents with errors clustered by country-year; the cell model on the panel by education band, which is built under the zero rule. Coefficient, with t in brackets. The first row is Table 3, Model 1, of OA. Source of the fitted rows: `companion/_model-outputs/claim2_fits.csv`."
fitted_rows <- claim2 |>
  datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "cosmo",
                          term %in% c("unemployment", "education: high", "mid x unemployment", "high x unemployment")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rule = dplyr::if_else(grepl("dropped", model), "no-opinion dropped", "no-opinion scored zero"),
                          design = dplyr::case_when(grepl("^published", model) ~ "published model, respondents",
                                                    level == "respondent"      ~ "fixed effects, respondents",
                                                    TRUE                       ~ "fixed effects, education-band cells"),
                          value = paste0(insight::format_value(estimate, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus", zap_small = TRUE), " (",
                                         insight::format_value(statistic, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"), ")")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("design", "rule", "term", "value")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = value) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("design", "rule"))
# the published values, transcribed from Table 3, Model 1, of the paper (pp. 626–627)
oa_row <- tibble::tibble(design = "OA, Table 3 Model 1", rule = "no-opinion dropped",
                         unemployment = "−0.0034 (−4.03)", `education: high` = "0.0771 (41.79)",
                         `mid x unemployment` = "−0.0014 (−3.23)", `high x unemployment` = "−0.0031 (−6.93)")
dplyr::bind_rows(oa_row, fitted_rows) |>
  dplyr::select(design, rule, unemployment, `education: high`, `mid x unemployment`, `high x unemployment`) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

```{r}
#| label: claim2-values
#| include: false
c2 <- claim2 |>
  datawizard::data_filter(outcome == "cosmo") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(design = dplyr::case_when(grepl("^published", model) ~ "published",
                                                    level == "respondent" ~ "fe_respondents",
                                                    TRUE ~ "fe_cells"),
                          rule = dplyr::if_else(grepl("dropped", model), "drop", "zero"),
                          key = paste(design, rule, term, sep = "|"))
c2_b <- stats::setNames(c2$estimate, c2$key)
c2_t <- stats::setNames(c2$statistic, c2$key)

# the education gap of the cell model under each unemployment series that
# covers all 270 country-years, from the committed series of the case study
series <- readr::read_csv("../data/macro/predictor_measures.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(predictor == "unemp", measure != "es_1574_tips")
gap_by_series <- purrr::map_dbl(unique(series$measure), \(ms) {
  d <- edu |>
    dplyr::left_join(series |>
                       dplyr::filter(measure == ms) |>
                       dplyr::select(cntry, year, value),
                     by = c("cntry", "year")) |>
    dplyr::mutate(munemp = value - mean(value), mgrowth = growth - mean(growth))
  coef(fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ edu3 * munemp + edu3 * mgrowth | cntry + year,
                     data = d, weights = ~n))[["edu3high"]]
})

# the interaction on the 810 cells under random intercepts, with and without
# the intercepts for country-years and the dummies for years
ri_cells <- list(
  cy      = mcosmo ~ edu3 * munemp + edu3 * mgrowth + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cy),
  cy_year = mcosmo ~ edu3 * munemp + edu3 * mgrowth + factor(year) + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cy),
  country = mcosmo ~ edu3 * munemp + edu3 * mgrowth + (1 | cntry)) |>
  purrr::map_dbl(\(f) lme4::fixef(lme4::lmer(f, data = edu, weights = n))[["edu3high:munemp"]])
```

The published design under the published rule reproduces the interaction of OA closely, `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["published|drop|high x unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` against −0.0031 in the paper, with a t of `r insight::format_value(c2_t[["published|drop|high x unemployment"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` against −6.93. The other terms of the row are further apart, the education gap `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["published|drop|education: high"]], digits = 4)` against 0.0771 and the unemployment slope `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["published|drop|unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` against −0.0034, and the change from the Eurostat unemployment series of the paper to the World Bank series of the course does not account for the gap: on the panel by education band, swapping one unemployment series for another moves the education gap by at most `r insight::format_value(diff(range(gap_by_series)), digits = 5)`. The refit also keeps `r format(oa_published$respondents, big.mark = ",")` respondents, where the note to Table 3 of the paper reports 335,566. That row is the reproduction, and it is the one to quote. The next row changes one thing, the rule for the respondents who named no item at all. The code of OA dropped them, because dividing by a total of zero mentions left them missing, and the course scores them zero on every scale, as three of the five analysts of the robustness study did, while KQXUE dropped them as OA had. The interaction then falls to `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["published|zero|high x unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")`. The respondents who name nothing are disproportionately low-educated, and scoring them zero pulls down the cosmopolitan mean of the low band in every cell in a way that does not move with unemployment, so the gap between the bands and its movement both change. A decision that the [module on scale construction](measurement.qmd#sec-noop-rules) classifies as a choice of measurement therefore moves the coefficient on which the claim rests.

The fixed-effects rows change the design instead. The fixed-effects design estimates a slope for unemployment as well as its difference between bands, because the national rate moves within each country from year to year and the country and year effects do not absorb it; under the published rule the slope is `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["fe_respondents|drop|unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` (t = `r insight::format_value(c2_t[["fe_respondents|drop|unemployment"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`), against `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["published|drop|unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` (t = `r insight::format_value(c2_t[["published|drop|unemployment"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`) in the published design, which repeats the finding of [section 7](#sec-designs), since the design of OA includes no year effects and unemployment and framing moved everywhere at once in 2009. The interaction under the published rule falls further with fixed effects, from `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["published|drop|high x unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["fe_respondents|drop|high x unemployment"]], digits = 4, style_negative = "minus")` (t = `r insight::format_value(c2_t[["fe_respondents|drop|high x unemployment"]], digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`), and under the zero rule it is practically zero, `r insight::format_value(c2_b[["fe_respondents|zero|high x unemployment"]], digits = 5, style_negative = "minus", style_positive = "plus")`. The cell row, fitted on 810 aggregates that anyone can download, agrees with the fixed-effects row of the respondents under the same rule on the unemployment slope and on both interactions, so for the interaction the aggregate route addresses the same question as the route through the respondents. Taken as a whole, the table shows the claim holding under the design and the rule that OA used, and weakening step by step as the fixed-effects design replaces the published one and as the respondents who named nothing are kept rather than dropped. Year effects shared by the three bands cannot remove a shock in which the bands moved differently, so what moves the interaction is the random intercepts for country-waves, which the fixed-effects rows drop: on the 810 cells a random-intercept model with intercepts for countries and country-years gives `r insight::format_value(ri_cells[["cy"]], digits = 5, style_negative = "minus")` without year effects and `r insight::format_value(ri_cells[["cy_year"]], digits = 5, style_negative = "minus")` with them, and `r insight::format_value(ri_cells[["country"]], digits = 5, style_negative = "minus", style_positive = "plus")` once the intercepts for country-years are removed.

The results reported in the paper include two qualifications that a replication should keep in view. The interaction holds for the cosmopolitan, communitarian and libertarian scales and not for the utilitarian one, where the "unemployment rate affects to the same extent the level of utilitarian framing of low-, middle-, and high-educated citizens" (p. 628). And the second sentence of the hypothesis, that the gap would move more on the materialist scales, is contradicted by the table of the paper itself: "in contrast to my hypothesis, the interactions between education and unemployment rate are no larger for the materialist dimensions of EU framing" (p. 628). The [measurement module](measurement.qmd#sec-theory) explains why that comparison presupposes a grouping that the data only half support. The other three outcomes are in the committed table for anyone who wants to check the first qualification against the real respondents:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-claim2-outcomes
#| tbl-cap: "The interaction of high education and unemployment on all four scales: Table 3, Model 1, of OA, and the published model refitted on the real respondents with the no-opinion respondents dropped, as the code of OA dropped them. Coefficient, with t in brackets. Source of the refitted values: `companion/_model-outputs/claim2_fits.csv`."
claim2 |>
  datawizard::data_filter(grepl("^published", model), grepl("dropped", model), term == "high x unemployment") |>
  dplyr::transmute(outcome,
                   refitted = paste0(insight::format_value(estimate, digits = 4, style_negative = "minus"), " (",
                                     insight::format_value(statistic, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"), ")")) |>
  # the published values, transcribed from Table 3, Model 1, of the paper (p. 627)
  dplyr::left_join(tibble::tibble(outcome = c("cosmo", "util", "comm", "lib"),
                                  published = c("−0.0031 (−6.93)", "−0.0004 (−1.73)", "0.0020 (5.63)", "0.0015 (4.84)")),
                   by = "outcome") |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("outcome", "published", "refitted")) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

The multilevel literature adds a caution about the standard error of such a term. @HeisigSchaeffer2019WhyYouShould [p. 258] argue that "multilevel models involving cross-level interactions should always include random slopes on the lower-level components of those interactions", because without them the test of the interaction is "severely anti-conservative", and @Stegmueller2013HowManyCountries [p. 748] finds that with few countries "maximum likelihood estimates and confidence intervals can be severely biased, especially in models including cross-level interactions", a warning that applies to the same term. The published model tests its interactions with random intercepts only. A footnote of the paper reports that "[r]andom slopes models show similar regression coefficients to the random intercept model" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 631, n. 3], but similar coefficients say nothing about the standard errors on which the verdict depends, so a random slope for education across countries is one of the decisions that a reanalysis of this claim has to make. [Section 9 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-interactions) shows on the respondents of the European Social Survey what a random slope of the lower-level variable does to the test of two cross-level interactions.

**A replication exercise of your own.** The pieces for a second exercise in the style of the first are all on this page: a claim card, an estimand statement, a public dataset on which the aggregate design runs in the browser lab or the workspace, the respondent file for anyone who built it, and the published values of OA to reproduce. The menu is smaller than the one for the first claim, and each of its decisions is one that you can defend or not: the frame set, the scoring rule, the rule for the respondents who named nothing, the coding of education (the published three bands, or four bands that keep students separate), the estimator (random intercepts, fixed effects, or cells), the random part (random intercepts alone, or a random slope for education across countries), the sample, the weight, and whether growth enters beside unemployment. Fix one specification in a preregistration, as in Task 5, then run it and set the interaction that you get against the rows of the table above. The table already shows that two of those decisions, the design and the rule for the respondents who named nothing, decide whether the claim is found.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Refit `m_edu` above with `edu3 * munemp` replaced by `edu3 * mgrowth` alone, and read the growth interactions against the claim in the paper that "GDP growth impacts mainly on the EU framing of low-educated citizens" (p. 619). In the workspace the 810 cells are `data/europeanisation_cy_edu.csv`, and section 6 of `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` rebuilds the same cells from your respondent file as `by_edu`. Either file needs `unemp` and `growth` centred on their means over the 810 rows, as this page centres them, before the fit.

Then put the interaction to the respondents themselves. Adding `edu3:munemp + edu3:mgrowth` to `m_cosmo` of section 5 turns it into the published model with its interactions under the zero rule, and its coefficient on `edu3high:munemp` should match the row of the published model with the no-opinion respondents scored zero in @tbl-claim2. Fit the model once more with `s_util` as the outcome, and read the interaction that the paper found absent.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The specification is the published Table 3, Model 1, of OA with its cross-level interactions dropped, taken from the Stata code that the author provided to the SCORE dossier [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]. Every model of the respondents was fitted once, locally, on the respondent file that the workspace builds from the sixteen GESIS waves, which is never committed and never redistributed; [the data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) explains that regime. The saved outputs of sections 3, 8 and 9 come from `fit_models.R`, the numbers of the three random structures of section 3 from `fit_person_multilevel.R`, the published model of section 5 and the prevalence gradient of section 6 from `fit_person_anchor.R`, the fits with terms for the years of section 7 from `fit_person_years.R`, the fits of the second claim in section 10 from `fit_claim2.R`, and the refits of the published design from `R/13_reference_marks.R`, all in the folder `companion/_model-outputs/` but the last. The models in the live code of the page are fitted when the page is built, on the panel and the panel by education band, both of which ship with the site, and the numbers of section 8 come from the panel of weights, `teney_panel_weights.csv`, and from the files of the curve and of its deviations, all in `data/` and written by the pipeline in `R/`.

The vocabularies of the four traditions, with the standard texts of each, are set side by side in [section 1 of the Immigration module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html#sec-vocabularies), and @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing record the conflicting definitions of fixed and random effects; for learning the models from the start, @SnijdersBosker2012MultilevelAnalysisIntroduction and Gelman and Hill are the textbooks. The models are fitted with lme4 and lmerTest [@BatesEtAl2015FittingLinearMixedeffects; @KuznetsovaEtAl2017LmerTestPackageTests], fixest [@BergeEtAl2026FastUserfriendlyEconometrics], glmmTMB [@BrooksEtAl2017GlmmTMBBalancesSpeed] and ordbetareg [@Kubinec2023OrderedBetaRegression], and the weighted models of section 8 with the survey package [@Lumley2004AnalysisComplexSurvey] and WeMix [@BaileyEtAl2023WeMixWeightedMixed]. The within–between model is argued for by @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects and @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects, and the cautions about few countries and cross-level interactions are those of @BryanJenkins2016MultilevelModellingCountry, @Stegmueller2013HowManyCountries and @HeisigSchaeffer2019WhyYouShould. @Rabe-HeskethSkrondal2006MultilevelModellingComplex and @Carle2009FittingMultilevelModels treat weights in multilevel models, and the weighting overview of the GESIS Eurobarometer Data Service [@GESISWeightingOverview] documents the weights of the Eurobarometer.
